newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks eke out gain.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks eke out gain.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks closed slightly higher Friday after jitters over rising long-term interest rates sent the market reeling in the last two days.
After a volatile session, the Dow Jones industrial average ended up 1.16 points at 6,304.87, steadying from back-to-back losses totalling 170 points. For the week, the Dow lost 77.07 points.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,418 to 1,033 on active volume of 454 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Right from the opening bell, the Dow charted a frenzied course, sliding more than 50 points only to reverse course and later surge to a 40-point gain.
"The final analysis is -- it's been a rocky week," said Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities.
Analysts said computerized programme trading spurred the volatility as the market tried to find its footing after being rocked by a rapid rise in long-term bond interest rates.
The bond market also helped to shore up stocks.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond rose 20/32, lowering its yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, to 6.58 percent from 6.62 percent at Thursday's close.

"Bonds are back up which definitely helped the market," said Ricky Harrington, technical analyst at Interstate/Johnson Lane. "This morning we had extreme volatility and that's been the case for eight or nine sessions now. That's likely to continue to be the case going into early 1997."

The Dow index briefly dipped in the afternoon after President Clinton played down fears that a stock market correction would hurt the economy. Some analysts, however, downplayed the signficance of Clinton's comments on the stock market.

"I think Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan has decided jawboning is better than using monetary policy and it looks like Clinton has decided to pick up on that," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist of Legg Mason Wood Walker.
"I don't think Clinton has the same credibility," he said. "People will view it as a political statement."
Last week, Greenspan rattled global markets after he said the central bank needed to be wary when "irrational exuberance" infects markets because that could end up damaging the economy.

Technology stocks were broadly lower as the sector took its cue from the drop in Intel's shares after this week's string of gains on upbeat comments by Wall Street analysts. Intel closed 4-1/2 lower at 132-3/8.

Oracle lost 3-1/4 to 44 after lower-than-expected results for the latest quarter. Micron was off 1 to 35-1/2, Iomega shed 1-1/4 to 18-3/4 and Microsoft fell 1 to 80. But International Business Machines Corp. added 3/4 to 152-3/8.

Among individual issues, Federal Express rose 1-1/2 to 41-5/8 after it posted higher quarterly profits and announced a temporary 2 percent surcharge to all express package shipments due to high fuel prices.
Quaker Oats added 2 to 37-1/8 on renewed speculation that it may shed its Snapple and Gatorade businesses. Quaker declined to comment on the rumours.

American Express fell 1/8 to 53-3/4 and Citicorp added 5/8 to 99-1/4. The Wall Street Journal reported that Citicorp held unsuccessful talks to acquire American Express. Citicorp declined comment and American Express said it was not engaged in talks with anyone regarding a sale of the firm or any part of the company.

Philip Morris lost 2-3/8 to 111-1/2 its first day of trading after going ex-dividend. A Florida judge ordered a lawsuit against the tobacco industry, which includes claims under the state's anti-racketeering laws, to go forward next June.
The Nasdaq Composite index fell 13.42 points to 1,284.91.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks was off 0.69 at 728.64. The American Stock Exchange index was off 3.05 to 576.06.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 0.22 to 384.07. The average share was down 3 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,072.699 down 18.876 or 0.27 percent.
